messages.content:
You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: The real interest rate hits a 20-year high, but the gold ETF rises to a seven-month peak: Gold has changed anchors!

TEXT:
Source: Jintou
The traditional relationship between the US 10-year real yield and gold is undergoing a clear change. Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, points out,
Even as real yields rise to more than 20-year highs, holdings in gold ETFs are still rebounding.
Last Friday, the US 10-year real yield rose to 2.63%, the highest level in over 20 years, up 76 basis points since the beginning of the year. At the same time, total holdings in gold-backed ETFs, having declined in the first half of 2026, are rising again.
Hansen stated that this divergence demonstrates that the long-standing inverse relationship between real yields and gold demand is weakening. In the past, rising real yields meant a higher opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest or dividends, usually putting pressure on gold prices .
From 2022 to 2023, aggressive rate hikes by the Federal Reserve pushed real yields up rapidly and investors reduced exposure by exiting gold ETFs. Yet gold prices remained resilient at the time, as strong central bank buying offset ETF investor selling. Hansen believes there is now a further shift. Real yields have climbed again, but gold ETFs have not experienced a new round of massive liquidation; instead, holdings continue to increase.
Fiscal risks are changing the logic of gold holdings
Hansen argues that one key reason is that investors are beginning to view long-term yields from a different perspective.
He states,
More and more investors may see rising long-term yields as signals of fiscal risk, increased government debt servicing costs, and financial stability issues, not just as the alternative holding cost to gold.
In this scenario, the allocation value of gold—as an asset outside the traditional financial system—may rise. Hansen points out that the current historically high and still-rising real yields have not put traditional downward pressure on gold.
He believes that continued central bank gold buying, the return of Western ETF buyers, and demand from Asian investors have jointly expanded gold’s investor base. Compared to 2022–2023, this demand has also become less sensitive to interest rates and yields.
After the Federal Reserve’s rate hike last week, Hansen believes gold’s performance indicates that a more hawkish monetary policy has already been largely priced in by the market. He states: “Heading into the weekend, gold seemed indifferent to the Fed’s rate hike.”
Hansen currently maintains a bullish outlook. He points out that despite precious metals’ recent weak performance,
gold-backed ETF holdings have risen to a 7-month high
, indicating demand that is less sensitive to interest rates still exists.
Central bank buyers are changing the gold market structure
Indrani De, Head of Global Investment Research at FTSE Russell, also believes that simply relying on yields to judge the gold trend is no longer sufficient.
She says that rising nominal and real yields do indeed increase the opportunity cost of gold, but central banks have become an increasingly important gold buyer. From 2000 to the global financial crisis, central banks were net sellers of gold overall and then turned net buyers, with the pace of purchases accelerating significantly in recent years.
Indrani says: “The scale of gold purchased by central banks in the past two or three years is more than twice the level between 2010 and 2021.”
Central banks’ allocation logic differs from ordinary investors. Indrani points out that official institutions do not typically reduce gold holdings in response to increased opportunity cost due to rising bond yields.
She says:
“We now have a large amount of gold demand coming from sources that are not sensitive to yields.”
In her view, this is an important reason why the relationship between gold and real yields is further decoupling.
This change is also reflected in the global reserves structure. Indrani notes that, based on current valuations, the total value of gold held by central banks worldwide now exceeds that in US Treasury securities.
Meanwhile, the dollar’s share of global foreign exchange reserves continues to fall, dropping from just over 70% at the turn of the century to about 55%–57% currently. However, Indrani does not believe this indicates the dollar is losing its dominant status.
She believes the dollar still lacks a comparable alternative in scale. The current change is more akin to a gradual diversification of reserve assets, driven by geopolitical and global economic shifts.
Indrani expects that the official sector will remain an important source of demand in the gold market. Although future purchases may be below the unusually high levels of recent years, Asian and Latin American central banks are still participating, and geopolitical uncertainty has not quickly faded.
